faq.q: Why does my brain like routines?
faq.a: Routines let your brain run on autopilot, which saves energy and feels safe because you know what comes next. That leaves more brain power for learning and fun.
asks: Why do I like doing things the same way?

faq.q: Why do I feel sad about a good change?
faq.a: Every change means leaving something behind, even when the new thing is exciting. Feeling a little sad about what you are losing is normal.
asks: Why am I sad when something good is happening?

faq.q: How can I cope with a big change?
faq.a: Keep some routines the same, find out what you can about the change, talk about your feelings, and be patient with yourself while you get used to it.
asks: How do I get used to change?

faq.q: Why do some people like change more than others?
faq.a: People have different personalities and experiences. Some love new things; others prefer the familiar. Both are fine, and anyone can get better at handling change.

faq.q: What if a change at home is really hard?
faq.a: Changes like parents separating, an illness or money worries can bring lots of feelings. They are not your fault. Talk to a trusted grown-up or a school counsellor.
asks: My parents are splitting up, how do I cope?

facts: A 2009 study at University College London found that new habits took about 66 days on average to become automatic, though it ranged from 18 to 254 days.
Habits and routines are handled partly by deep brain areas called the basal ganglia, which frees the thinking brain for other things.
